sens: Edible jumping insect from the Middle East
Frugal food of desert hermits
Eschatological plague creature
G0200.detail: 1. The grasshopper is a well-known insect in Palestine, capable of jumping and flying. It is part of the diet of the peoples of the Middle East and North Africa, where it was eaten roasted, dried, or ground into powder. John the Baptist fed on locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4, Mark 1:6), a testament to his ascetic lifestyle in the desert. 2. In John the Baptist's case, locusts symbolize abstinence and detachment from earthly goods. It is a humble, simple food found locally without agricultural labor, highlighting the stripped-down nature of his life. It contrasts with banquets and shows the austerity of the one who prepares the way of the Lord. 3. In Revelation, locusts become supernatural and terrifying creatures emerging from the smoke of the abyss (Revelation 9:3, 7). They resemble war horses with crowns of gold and human faces: they are no longer ordinary insects, but agents of divine judgment at the end of times.
G0200.origine: The Greek word akris (ἀκρίς) is a simple and concrete term, attested to designate the insect since antiquity. In Greek, it regularly translates the Hebrew word arbé (אַרְבֶּה), which also refers to the locust. The latter is closely linked to the plagues of Egypt and biblical afflictions. The exact root and etymology of the Greek remain debated, but the word is still commonly used for this insect.
G0200.emploi: The word locust appears four times in the New Testament, all in the Gospels and Revelation. Matthew and Mark use it twice each to describe the food of John the Baptist in the desert, emphasizing his asceticism and preparation for ministry. In Revelation 9:3 and 7, the term completely shifts its register: locusts are no longer ordinary insects, but mythical creatures sent as an eschatological plague, symbolizing forces of divine destruction. Revelation describes them with hybrid traits (horses, crowns, human faces), suggesting a symbolic vision rather than a natural description. The contrast between the humble usage in Matthew-Mark and the apocalyptic usage shows how an ordinary word can shift towards spiritual realities.
G0200.portee: For the Christian, the locust first reminds us that renouncing earthly comforts is a path to spiritual freedom. John the Baptist, living on locusts, shows that the essence is not the table, but the presence of God. In Revelation, it teaches us that God has all means for judgment and purification: no creature escapes Him. These two aspects invite a simple and vigilant life, aware of the coming judgment.

sens: Place where one listens, where one sits to hear and judge
Room or court intended to receive pleadings and accusations
Court or official place of judgment
G0201.detail:
1. The word describes a room or space specially arranged for listening: it is a place where people gather to hear someone speak officially. In Acts 25:23, Festus the Roman governor brings Paul before him in the "place of hearing" — a room where court is held unofficially, in the presence of King Agrippa and Queen Berenice, along with all the dignitaries of the city.
2. It is a judicial space: the "hearing" is the context where the public examination of a case takes place, where accusers can present their grievances and the accused can defend themselves. Paul must respond to the accusations of the Jews before the Roman authorities.
G0201.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to listen" — the very root of the word "acroate" (one who listens, the auditor). The suffix constructs a place: it is therefore "the place where one listens." This formation recalls how Greek creates place names from verbs: just as a "school" is "a place where children are held," a "place of hearing" is naturally "a place where official words are heard."
G0201.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:23. Paul, imprisoned in Caesarea and accused by the Jewish authorities, is presented before Governor Festus and King Agrippa in this formal setting. It is a Roman administrative term: it designates the official reception room where authority sits to hear a plea or judgment. The context shows that it is a solemn place, with ceremony, in the presence of high-ranking personalities.
G0201.portee: This passage reveals how God placed the apostle Paul before the highest Roman and royal authorities — not for him to be condemned, but for the Gospel to be heard by those with the most power. The "place of hearing" becomes the stage for this wonderful reversal: the one who seemed weak and imprisoned becomes a witness of Jesus before the powerful of the world.

sens: one who listens
one who receives teaching without putting it into practice
one who hears the word of God
G0202.detail:
1. In the simplest sense, a listener is one who listens: it is someone to whom one speaks, who receives words. In Romans 2:13, Paul distinguishes those who "listen" to the law (the listeners) from those who put it into practice.
2. The word takes on a critical nuance when it designates one who is content to hear without acting: it is the image of the mirror in James 1:23-25. A "forgetful" listener looks at the word, perhaps understands it, but immediately turns away, like someone who looks at themselves in a mirror and then goes away without changing anything about their appearance.
3. In the spiritual context, the listener of the word of God is called not to remain passive. James 1:22 warns: do not merely listen, or you deceive yourselves — true happiness comes from the one who puts into practice what they have heard (James 1:25).
G0202.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "to listen" (akouō). A listener is literally one who "listens to the end." This word appears in the New Testament to describe a relationship to the word: one is not just a passerby who hears sounds, but someone who receives a message, whether understood or not.
G0202.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, all in passages that emphasize the importance of putting into practice what one hears. Paul uses it in Romans 2:13 to show that before God, what matters is obedience, not just listening. James returns to this same theme three times (1:22-25): he warns against the illusion of being a "listener" who believes they are transformed by simply listening. The emphasis is always on the contrast between listening and doing.
G0202.portee: This word calls every Christian to examine their own relationship to the word of God. Going to church, reading the Bible, listening to a sermon: this is good, but it is only a beginning. True faith is tested in concrete obedience. The forgetful listener is not an unbeliever, but someone who misses the grace of God by not allowing the word to transform their life.

sens: The foreskin, the skin that covers the glans in men
The state of one who has not undergone circumcision
The separation between circumcised Jews and uncircumcised non-Jews
What is external and carnal, in contrast to what is internal and spiritual
G0203.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the foreskin itself, the physical part of the body — this is the medical and concrete sense of the term (Romans 4:10, where Abraham was 'uncircumcised' before circumcision).
2. By extension, it designates the general state of one who has not received circumcision, who has never undergone it — a physical and identity condition (Acts 11:3, where the apostles reproach Peter for eating with 'uncircumcised' individuals).
3. The word takes on a social and religious significance: it opposes two groups, the circumcised (Jews of the covenant) and the uncircumcised (Gentiles). This is a very important community boundary in the life of the early churches (Romans 3:30, where God justifies 'by faith the circumcised, and by faith the uncircumcised').
4. In Paul, uncircumcision becomes especially a symbol: what is external, carnal, superficial, without connection to faith. Only faith in Christ matters, not the physical sign (1 Corinthians 7:19: 'Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God is what matters').
G0203.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning 'the part of the end' or 'the extremity' (akron) and 'skin' or 'membrane'. It translates the Hebrew ʿorlah (foreskin), which refers to the Old Testament: everything that is not circumcised is 'ritually unclean'. The Hebrew root ʿorlah is linked to the idea of a barrier, a layer that separates. For the Jews, circumcision was the sign of the covenant with God; not having it marked a distance from the chosen people.
G0203.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul (Romans and Galatians) and in Acts. In Acts 11, it simply refers to the uncircumcised Gentiles, with whom Peter should not eat according to Jewish law. In Paul (Romans 2—4), the word takes on a strong theological charge: Paul argues that the uncircumcised who keeps the law is better than the circumcised who transgresses it, and that true circumcision is that of the heart, not of the body. In 1 Corinthians 7:19 and Galatians 5:6, Paul declares that circumcision has no value; only faith in Christ and keeping the commandments matter. In Ephesians 2:11 and Colossians 3:11, uncircumcision completely fades away in the Church, for Christ has reconciled Jews and Gentiles.
G0203.portee: This word reveals the great turning point of the Christian faith: what mattered for religious identity — the physical sign of the covenant — loses all value in light of faith in Jesus Christ. For today's Christian, uncircumcision reminds us that God does not look at external signs, appearances, or social statuses. What matters is the heart transformed by faith, trust in Christ, and obedience to His commandments, not carnal practices or distinctions. It is an invitation to look beyond the barriers of this world.

sens: Stone placed at the extreme angle of a construction, which unites the walls
Main foundation of a building, which ensures its stability
Person or principle that unites and supports a community
One in whom rests the trust and hope of salvation
G0204.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a stone located at the extreme angle of a building, where two walls meet. This 'cornerstone' is visible from all sides and structurally unites the walls that join it (Ephesians 2:20).
2. It is also the capital foundation on which the entire construction rests: without this cornerstone, the whole building would be unstable. It bears the weight and ensures the cohesion of the whole (1 Peter 2:6).
3. The Bible uses this image for the Church: Jesus Christ is the 'cornerstone' that unites Jews and Gentiles into one body, with believers being 'built' on Him as living stones.
4. More broadly, this word also evokes the person on whom one bases their hope, in whom one places absolute trust. In Jesus rests all the promises of salvation; that is why the Bible cites Isaiah 28:16: 'he who believes in it will not be put to shame' (1 Peter 2:6).
G0204.origine: The Greek word combines two ideas: 'akron' (extremity, summit) and 'gonia' (angle). It is an adjective that literally means 'situated at the angular extremity'. This architectural image comes from the practice of construction: the cornerstone was often the largest, the strongest, and the most visible, as it had to support the weight of two walls. The word translates the Hebrew 'pinnah' (angle, corner) used in the messianic prophecies of the Old Testament, notably Isaiah 28:16.
G0204.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, exclusively in Ephesians 2:20 and 1 Peter 2:6, where it refers to Jesus Christ. Both passages are citations or allusions to the prophecy of Isaiah 28:16 about the stone that God lays in Zion. In Ephesians 2:20, Paul uses it to explain how the Church — composed of Jews and non-Jews — is a single building of which Jesus is the fundamental 'cornerstone'. In 1 Peter 2:6, Peter takes up the same prophecy to encourage persecuted believers: he who believes in this stone will not be disappointed. The context is always Christological (concerning Christ) and ecclesiological (concerning the Church).
G0204.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand the unique importance of Jesus Christ for the Church and for their own faith. Just as a cornerstone unites and stabilizes a house, Jesus unites believers into one body and establishes their eternal trust. It is a powerful image: building one's life on Christ is to place it on the most solid foundation. For those who doubt or suffer, this 'cornerstone' reminds us that our salvation does not rest on our strengths or circumstances, but on the very person of Jesus.

sens: The best part of the spoil taken from the enemy in battle
What is excellent or of first quality among the spoils of war
G0205.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the top of a heap, then by extension the best part of the spoil captured in war — what warriors considered the most precious. In Hebrews 7:4, Abraham gives a tithe of the 'spoil' taken after defeating the kings: it is therefore the best of what had been conquered. 2. By figurative usage, the term can also designate what is best or most excellent in a whole, like the first fruits of a harvest. It conveys the idea of choice, of what is above the rest.
G0205.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: 'akron' (the summit, the peak) and 'this' (a heap, a pile). The starting image is that of the top of a pile, what naturally comes out and is well visible. This image has been applied to the spoils of war: the best of the spoil, that which is set aside, is 'at the top' of the conquered riches. The Hebrew word that the Septuagint translates this way is often 'shalal' (spoil) or 'resit' (first fruits, first part).
G0205.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 7:4. The author uses it to highlight the greatness of Abraham: this patriarch gave a tithe — that is, one-tenth — of the most precious spoil he had won from his enemies. This act demonstrates his devotion to God and enhances the honor of Melchizedek, the priest to whom Abraham gave this offering. The warrior context and the idea of exceptional generosity mark this unique usage.
G0205.portee: This word shows that Abraham, although victorious and enriched by war, recognized that the best of his gains did not belong to him alone: he offered it to God through the hands of the priest. For the reader, this teaches that true greatness is not in possession but in giving: even the spoil of war, a mark of personal victory, must honor God first.

sens: The part that ends, which delimits an object
The point or the summit
The tip of a finger or a limb
The borders of a region or a space
G0206.detail:
1. Extremity refers to the final or terminal part of something, marking its end and limits — like the tip of a stick on which Jacob leans (Hebrews 11:21), or the tip of Lazarus' finger that the poor man asks Abraham for (Luke 16:24).
2. The word can evoke the highest point or the tip of something, its extreme limit upwards — which was its primitive meaning in Greek (‘the highest’).
3. Applied to the body, extremity refers to the limbs that extend far away: a finger that sticks out, a raised hand, a part of the body that is distant from the center.
4. Geographically, the word describes the borders, the extreme limits of a region — ‘from the four winds, from one extremity of heaven to the other’ (Matthew 24:31) or ‘from the extremity of the earth to the extremity of heaven’ (Mark 13:27), speaking of the boundaries of the created world.
G0206.origine: The Greek word ἄκρον comes from the adjective ἄκρος, which originally meant ‘extreme’, ‘at the summit’, ‘at the limits’. It is a term that describes what is farthest away, most distant, most forward — hence the name ἄκρον to designate the tip, the end, what protrudes. It is related to many words denoting the extremities of the body (acromion, acronym in modern French). In the Greek Old Testament, it translates several Hebrew words concerning extremities or high points: קֶצַח (the bald part of the skull), בֹּהֶן (the thumb or big toe).
G0206.emploi: The word ἄκρον appears four times in the New Testament, always to describe an extremity, but in very varied contexts. In the three synoptic gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it designates the confines of the cosmos — the extremities of heaven and earth at the four corners of the world, when the angels will gather the elect on the day of judgment (Matthew 24:31 and Mark 13:27). It is a majestic and cosmic use of the word. In Luke 16:24, on the contrary, it is the concrete and miserable application: the tip of the poor man's finger that could refresh the rich man's tongue in torment. And in Hebrews 11:21, it is the tip of the stick on which Jacob leans before dying — a touching detail of the patriarch's gesture of blessing. The word thus oscillates between the immense (the confines of heaven and earth) and the minute (the tip of a finger, the tip of a stick).
G0206.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the cosmic scope of the divine plan: on the day of judgment, the angels will gather the elect ‘from the four winds’, to the extreme limits of the created world, showing that God is master of the entire universe down to its last borders. But it also reminds us that God sees and judges every minute detail — the tip of a poor man's finger, the gesture of an elderly man who, dying, blesses his children — from the greatest to the smallest, nothing escapes His knowledge and love.

sens: Jew from Pontus, tentmaker
Companion of the apostle and teacher of the way of God
Head of a household that hosts the church
G0207.detail:
1. Aquila is a Jew from Pontus (a region on the northern coast of Asia Minor) who, forced to leave Rome by the edict of Emperor Claudius, settled in Corinth with his wife Priscilla (Acts 18:2). He worked as a tentmaker, which allowed Paul to work with him and live alongside them.
2. He is presented as a companion in apostolic work: Paul mentions him among his ‘fellow workers in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 16:3). Together with Priscilla, he accurately taught the way of God to Apollos, whom they had heard preaching incompletely in Ephesus (Acts 18:26).
3. Aquila and Priscilla formed a couple of hospitality: their home hosted the assembly of believers, as indicated by the greeting ‘the church that is in their house’ (1 Corinthians 16:19), and Paul sends them a personal greeting (2 Timothy 4:19).
G0207.origine: The name Aquila (Ἀκύλας) is the Greek form of the Latin Aquila, which literally means ‘eagle’ — a common Roman family name. Although of Latin origin (suggesting perhaps a Roman ancestry or a close proximity to Roman culture), Aquila was Jewish by birth and respectful of the Law, as shown by his adherence to the emerging Christian movement.
G0207.emploi: Aquila appears six times in the New Testament, always alongside his wife Priscilla. The couple plays a discreet but valuable role in the Acts and the epistles: first encountered by Paul in Corinth, where the three share the same trade, he later travels with Paul to Syria (Acts 18:18), settles in Ephesus where he teaches Apollos (Acts 18:26), and then appears in Rome where Paul sends him greetings (Romans 16:3, 1 Corinthians 16:19, 2 Timothy 4:19). He is an example of a Christian couple active in the local church, not apostles in the official sense, but faithful and hospitable teachers.
G0207.portee: Aquila and Priscilla embody the model of ordinary yet decisive ministry: working with their hands, sharing their faith, hosting the assembly in their home, gently correcting a gifted but incomplete speaker. Their example encourages believers to see that effectiveness in the kingdom of God does not come only from great apostles, but also from the humble availability of couples and households who dedicate their home, time, and knowledge to the service of the Gospel.

sens: Render ineffective, invalidate
Render null or inoperative
Reduce to nothing, make vain
G0208.detail:
1. Annul means to render something without value or effect. The Pharisees annul the word of God by prioritizing their human traditions (Matthew 15:6, Mark 7:13): their teachings contradict and stifle the authority of what God has said.
2. The word can also mean to render a previous provision or commitment null and void. Paul states that the Law, which came four hundred thirty years after the promise made to Abraham, cannot annul that promise or make it void (Galatians 3:17): the promise remains firm despite the arrival of the Law.
3. It is to render something ineffective or stripped of its power: to reduce to nothing the strength or authority that a word or agreement possessed.
G0208.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ‘kyros’ which means ‘authority’ or ‘power of decision’. The prefix ‘a-’ (privative) gives ἀκυρόω the literal sense of ‘to take away the authority from’. It is the opposite of making valid or confirming. The central notion is that of an authority that is suppressed or revoked.
G0208.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always in contexts of opposition or invalidation. In Matthew 15:6 and Mark 7:13, Jesus denounces those who annul the authority of the word of God by contradicting it with human traditions — it is a grave act of substituting authorities. In Galatians 3:17, Paul exposes a theological principle: no law or covenant subsequent can annul a prior and confirmed divine commitment. The context changes but the meaning remains constant: to remove the validity or normative weight of something.
G0208.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the authority of the word of God cannot be surpassed or invalidated by any human tradition or subsequent law. It raises a question of faithfulness: do our practices and teachings annul the word of God? It invites us to examine where we truly seek our authority.

sens: Free from any obstruction, without restriction or impediment
With freedom of action, without fear of retaliation
G0209.detail:
1. The word describes an action that unfolds without any material or legal obstacles. Paul preaches in Rome "with all boldness and without hindrance" (Acts 28:31): no one stops him, he is not hindered in his proclamation of the Gospel.
2. It is also a freedom that comes from the absence of threat or restriction: acting without fear that someone or something will stop you. Paul's preaching continues freely, despite the political and religious obstacles that could have restrained it.
G0209.origine: The word comes from the Greek root κωλύω (to hinder, to restrain) preceded by the privative prefix ἀ- (which negates or denies). Literally, "without hindrance." This formation, common in Greek legal documents to speak of an action devoid of legal restrictions, expresses the idea of freedom and absence of hindrance.
G0209.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:31, at the end of the Acts narrative. Paul arrives in Rome as a prisoner, but the text emphasizes that he "preaches the kingdom of God and teaches concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, with all boldness and without hindrance." Despite the chains that physically bind him, his word remains free: no Roman authority prevents him from proclaiming the Gospel. This final detail of Acts reveals the paradoxical victory of faith: even in captivity, the witness of Christ enjoys a spiritual freedom that no one can take away.
G0209.portee: This word invites the reader to see that true freedom does not depend on external circumstances, but on the testimony one bears. Paul, chained, preaches more freely than many free men. He reminds us that the one who obeys God and proclaims His Gospel possesses an inner freedom that the world cannot give or take away. For today's Christian, it is a promise: the word of God advances unhindered, despite apparent obstacles.

sens: Against one's will, unintentionally
Under compulsion or obligation
In spite of personal reluctance
G0210.detail:
1. The word describes an action done against one's own will, without having chosen it: one acts, but does not want to. Paul uses it when he says that if he preaches the Gospel "against" his will, meaning without having chosen it freely, he does not receive a reward for it (1 Corinthians 9:17).
2. It is an action accomplished out of obligation or external compulsion, not by personal desire. Paul's contrast is clear: preaching willingly brings a reward, but preaching against one's will, out of mere imposed duty, is "a stewardship entrusted to me."
3. The word emphasizes inner reluctance: one acts, but without heartfelt agreement, almost regretfully.
G0210.origine: The Greek word comes from a negation (a-) and a root meaning "to will," "to consent": it literally means "unwilling." It contrasts with the Greek "hékon" (willing, consenting). In Hebrew, translations of the Old Testament Greek use similar words to express constraint and the involuntary.
G0210.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 9:17. Paul uses it to address a personal question: does he receive a reward for his apostolic ministry? He distinguishes between two cases — acting willingly (hékōn) or against one's will (akōn) — and shows that only the voluntary commitment of the heart entitles one to the reward. It is a rare but decisive word to show the importance Paul places on moral freedom and authentic love in Christian service.
G0210.portee: This word invites the Christian to examine their heart: do you act out of true love or mere obligation? God looks not only at the act but at the will that drives it. This encourages serving willingly, not "against one's will," so that our obedience is joyful and worthy of reward.

sens: Container made of alabaster, a white and translucent stone
Small jar or flask intended to hold precious perfumes and ointments
Figuratively: valuable and intimate offering to someone
G0211.detail:
1. An alabaster jar is a container shaped from a soft, white stone, alabaster, which was highly valued in antiquity for its beauty and rarity. This noble material is suitable for luxury items.
2. These jars were primarily used to preserve and pour expensive perfumes and precious ointments, as shown by the example of the woman in Luke 7:37 who "brought an alabaster jar full of perfume." It was an elegant and hermetically sealed container, worthy of holding rare and costly substances.
3. In the Gospel, the alabaster jar becomes the symbol of a personal and humble offering: the sinful woman breaks her jar at Jesus' feet (Mark 14:3), thus expressing sincere repentance and unreserved love. It is an act of intimacy and total devotion.
G0211.origine: The word comes from the Greek alabastron, itself borrowed from an ancient Near Eastern language (possibly Egyptian). The name designates both the material — alabaster, a translucent white or slightly colored stone — and the jar made from it. The word appears in the Greek Old Testament to translate the Hebrew word צַלַּחַת (tsallachat), which means "bowl" or "dish" (2 Kings 21:13). The form is attested in several variations in common and popular Greek.
G0211.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, only in the Synoptic Gospels, to designate the container that a woman breaks at Jesus' feet. In Matthew 26:7, it is "an alabaster jar" that "contained very costly perfume." Mark 14:3 specifies that it contained "pure nard, very costly" and that the woman "broke the jar" and poured it on Jesus' head. Luke 7:37 reports the same scene with a sinful woman. The three Gospels agree on the preciousness of the jar and the perfume, emphasizing that this act was a valuable offering, a symbol of authentic love and devotion towards Jesus.
G0211.portee: This alabaster jar embodies a profound truth: those who welcome Jesus in humility and love do not hesitate to spend freely to express their gratitude and faith. The breaking of the jar symbolizes total self-abandonment, the personal sacrifice that accepts losing what is most precious. It is an invitation for the reader to reflect on the value of their own offering to God and the authenticity of their love for Christ.

sens: The habit of boasting, speaking of oneself excessively and presumptuously
The attitude of one who exaggerates their importance, merits, or worth
Excessive self-confidence and reliance on one's possessions
The love of earthly glory and honors, contrary to Christian humility
G0212.detail:
1. It is primarily the habit of glorifying or boasting without measure: in James 4:16, those who make business plans without considering God "boast in your arrogant thoughts," meaning they indulge in an exaggerated self-esteem and their projects.

2. More broadly, it is an excessive confidence in one's own strengths, wealth, or appearance: in 1 John 2:16, the "pride of life" refers to the attitude of one who believes they are great and important because of what they possess or the image they project — it is one of the three elements of the world system that opposes God, alongside the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes.

3. Therefore, it is the opposite of humility: this pride arises when one forgets that everything comes from God and places oneself at the center of their thoughts and plans.
G0212.origine: The word comes from the name ἀλαζών (alazôn), which designates a braggart or boaster — someone who constantly exaggerates their exploits and qualities. It is a typical character in Greek comedy, a figure of ridicule. The name ἀλαζονεία thus designates the character, the habitual attitude of this braggart. The Greek word conveys the idea of a false appearance, a pretense that swells without real foundation.
G0212.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament. In James 4:16, it describes the attitude of people who make ambitious plans while forgetting God — it is a practical pride, that of business life. In 1 John 2:16, it refers to the "pride of life," one of the three traps of the world: it is the pride of appearances and possessions. In both cases, the Bible presents it as something bad and dangerous for the Christian.
G0212.portee: This word reminds us that pride — especially that which manifests itself through boasting or complacency in one's own strengths — is a serious sin in the eyes of God. It invites us to recognize that everything we have and all that we are comes from God, and to reject this worldly mentality that would have us believe that we can succeed by our own strength or that our worth depends on our possessions.

sens: One who boasts, who glorifies themselves in an exaggerated and often deceptive manner.
One who acts important, displaying a false superiority to impress others.
One who speaks boldly but without true foundation.
G0213.detail:
1. A braggart is someone who boasts without restraint: they exaggerate their qualities, exploits, or possessions to make themselves look good. In Romans 1:30, Paul lists the faults of men far from God, and the braggart is mentioned alongside slanderers and the proud.
2. It is also one who seeks to dominate through hollow words and an affected attitude of superiority. They talk a lot, promise a lot, but lack substance: in 2 Timothy 3:2, Paul warns Timothy about men of the last days who are selfish, arrogant, and braggarts, people without true moral depth.
3. The word evokes the image of a vagabond who travels the roads telling stories about themselves to gain admiration — hence the notion of imposture and deception that accompanies it.
G0213.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "vagabond" (from ἄλη, which means "wandering"). By extension, it designates one who wanders while telling stories, a charlatan, an impostor. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses this word to translate Hebrew terms describing the arrogant and the vain: the proud who elevate themselves without true foundation.
G0213.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's epistles. In Romans 1:30, it is mentioned in a catalog of sins that characterize humanity rebelling against God. In 2 Timothy 3:2, it appears in a list of vices that will mark men in the last days — people concerned with themselves, loving money, and eager for power. In both contexts, the braggart is presented as a characteristic human type of one who strays from virtue and the fear of God. The word emphasizes less an isolated sin than a heart attitude: the pretense of a greatness that one does not possess.
G0213.portee: Identifying the braggart within oneself helps the believer examine their heart: do they seek to impress, to promote themselves, to exaggerate their merits? The Bible invites us to simplicity and humility before God and others. Recognizing this sin and rejecting it is a step toward greater integrity and truth in our relationships.

sens: To shout loudly, to raise one's voice intensely and suddenly
To express emotion through cries, whether of joy, fear, or mourning
To produce a loud and resonant sound
G0214.detail:
1. This verb depicts the action of crying out loudly, letting out an exclamation that fills the space. In Mark 5:38, the people around Jairus's house cry out loudly while weeping: it is the raw expression of grief and emotional turmoil in the face of the child's death.
2. The word captures the cry as a visceral expression of what one feels: fear, pain, or triumph. It depicts less the words than the noise itself, the fact that the feeling explodes into sounds.
3. In 1 Corinthians 13:1, Paul speaks of a cymbal that "resounds": the verb then describes the clanging sound of metal, without meaning or content, pure noise that strikes the ear. It is an empty sound that communicates nothing, an image of absent charity.
G0214.origine: The word is onomatopoeic: "alalá" imitates the war or jubilation cry that was shouted in antiquity. This sound imitation of the cry itself primarily expresses a warlike or festive acclamation before being applied to any intense cry. The family of the word in Greek shows that the central idea is the loud noise, the sound manifestation of an emotion or circumstance.
G0214.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Mark 5:38, it designates the cry of the mourners and the bereaved at Jairus's house: a cry of mourning and confusion in the face of death. In 1 Corinthians 13:1, Paul uses it for a resounding cymbal: the verb loses connotation of fear or sorrow and simply depicts a loud but hollow sound. These two uses show that the word primarily captures the sound force, the external manifestation, the raw intensity of the voice or noise, regardless of the emotion underlying it.
G0214.portee: This word reminds us that the expression of our feelings has power: it resonates, it is heard. In Mark 5:38, those who cry out testify to their human distress in the face of death. In 1 Corinthians 13:1, Paul warns that all our gifts, without charity, are just empty noise: the cry without love means nothing. This contrast invites us to ensure that our faith and actions arise from true love, not just emotional spectacle.

sens: That which cannot be expressed in words
That which exceeds the capacities of language
That which is too deep or too great to be put into words
G0215.detail:
1. The word describes what cannot be said, stated, or communicated by ordinary language. In Romans 8:26, the Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groans: these are sighs so deep, so laden with divine meaning, that no human words could translate or contain them.
2. More broadly, it refers to what exceeds our ability to formulate, what goes beyond what our words can grasp or express. The idea emphasizes a limit: we lack vocabulary, or the reality is too vast, too subtle, or too holy to fit into human language.
3. In a spiritual context, the word evokes the inexpressible beauty, greatness, or intensity of a divine experience — something authentic and powerful that stirs our hearts but leaves us speechless.
G0215.origine: The Greek word ἀλάλητος is composed of the privative prefix ἀ- ("not," "without") and the verb λαλέω (lalèô, "to speak," "to say"). Literally, it means "that which cannot be spoken" or "of which one cannot speak." The root evokes the act of speaking, of producing articulated sounds — and the prefix negates this possibility. The word is rare in classical ancient Greek; it primarily arises in biblical vocabulary to express what escapes the limits of human language.
G0215.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:26. Paul uses it to describe the intercession of the Holy Spirit before God the Father: this Spirit prays "with inexpressible groans" on our behalf. This context shows us that the inexpressible is not a flaw or an absence, but rather a sign of a spiritual reality that is too deep, too holy, too laden with divine meaning to be reduced to words. That is why the Spirit Himself must intervene: He knows our weakness and our inability to express what we ought to ask for.
G0215.portee: This word comforts the believer who feels awkward or helpless in prayer. It reminds us that God does not judge us based on the elegance or clarity of our words, but that the Holy Spirit intercedes for us with a depth that our lips cannot articulate. It invites us to stop fearing our "poorly said" prayers: the sincere groan, the sigh of the heart, the inexpressible longing for God — all of this is heard and transformed by the Spirit into perfect prayer.

sens: One who cannot speak
One who is rendered unable to speak by a force or illness
One who remains silent, voiceless
G0216.detail:
1. The word designates one who is deprived of speech, who cannot produce articulated sound. In Mark 7:37, the crowd marvels that Jesus "makes the mute speak," meaning He restores the ability to speak to those who were deprived of it.
2. In several cases, this inability to speak is caused by an evil power: the spirit that possesses the boy in Mark 9:17 and 9:25 is described as "mute," because it renders the boy unable to utter words. The context shows that this is a demonic oppression that takes away the voice.
3. More broadly, the word can refer to one who is silenced, deprived of speech for any reason, physical or spiritual.
G0216.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "not to speak" (privative prefix α- and λάλος "one who speaks"). It is the opposite of a chatterer: while λάλος refers to one who speaks easily, ἄλαλος refers to one to whom all speech is denied. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the same meaning is found in words like אִלֵּם (illem), "mute" or "voiceless."
G0216.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Gospel of Mark, and always in contexts of healing or demonic possession. In Mark 7:37, it refers to a general healing: Jesus makes the deaf hear and the mute speak, demonstrating His power over human infirmities. In Mark 9:17 and 9:25, the evil spirit that possesses the child is expressly called "mute," suggesting that the demon renders mute the one it dominates, depriving them of speech. The context reveals that this muteness is not a mere physical infirmity, but a symptom of demonic oppression.
G0216.portee: For the believer, these passages show that Jesus has authority over all that takes away voice and human freedom: illness, infirmity, evil power. The miracle of restoring speech to the mute symbolizes the restored integrity of the person and their ability to express themselves fully. It is also an image of spiritual deliverance: the one who is freed can finally speak, shout, and testify.

sens: Crystallized white mineral that preserves food and enhances its flavor
Wisdom and grace in speech
Quality of one who preserves and spiritually fertilizes
G0217.detail:
1. Salt is the white, crystallized mineral used to season and preserve food. It is a precious commodity recognized by all. Jesus uses this ordinary image to speak of the influence of believers: "You are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13).
2. Salt loses its flavor when it is altered or corrupted — this is impossible in nature, but possible in a figurative sense for the salt of the earth, meaning for disciples who would abandon their mission or faithfulness. Once useless, "it is good for nothing but to be thrown out and trampled underfoot" (Matthew 5:13).
3. In the realm of speech, salt represents wisdom and grace in speaking. Paul advises: "Let your speech always be seasoned with grace, as with salt" (Colossians 4:6) — meaning a wise, pleasant word, capable of "adding flavor" to conversation and preserving what is good.
G0217.origine: The Greek word for "salt" (halas) derives from classical Greek that designates this mineral. In Hebrew, "melah" (מְלַח) carries the same meaning and symbolic significance. In ancient times, salt was a very valuable commodity, used for preserving, seasoning, and even consecrating (salt appears in the sacrifices of Israel's worship). This value explains why Jesus chooses it as an image of the lasting and fertilizing influence of believers.
G0217.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in the three Synoptic Gospels and in Paul. In Matthew 5:13, Mark 9:50, and Luke 14:34, Jesus uses salt in both a literal and figurative sense: the literal salt that seasons and preserves becomes the image of disciples who "season" the world through their faithful presence and testimony. The image of lost flavor underscores the irony: if salt becomes tasteless, it loses all its interest. In Colossians 4:6, Paul extends the image to speech itself: a "salty" word is a wise, gracious, and pleasant word to listen to, capable of preserving harmony among Christians.
G0217.portee: The image of salt teaches the believer that their presence in the world should have a positive and lasting influence, just as salt preserves and enhances what it mingles with. It also calls for vigilance: losing its flavor risks becoming useless and being rejected. In terms of speech, it encourages the disciple to speak with wisdom and grace, like someone who "seasons" the conversation rather than spoiling it.

sens: To apply oil or perfume to the body or a part of the body
To apply a fragrant or medicinal substance to someone as a sign of respect or care
To prepare a body for burial by anointing it with precious spices
G0218.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to apply oil or perfume to the body or a part of the body. This is a common daily gesture in the East: one would anoint after bathing, during festive occasions, or for well-being. Jesus rebukes the Pharisee: "You did not anoint my head with oil" (Luke 7:46), which would have been the courteous welcome due to an honored guest.
2. The word also refers to the application of oil for care or healing. The disciples "anointed many sick people with oil and healed them" (Mark 6:13), and James prescribes: "Let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord" (James 5:14), where anointing accompanies prayer for healing.
3. Finally, to anoint can mean to prepare a body for burial by anointing it with precious spices. The women buy spices "to anoint Jesus" (Mark 16:1): this is an act of honor and love towards the deceased.
G0218.origine: The Greek verb ἀλείφω comes from a root related to oil (λίπος in Greek means fat or oil). It often translates the Hebrew סוּךְ (sûk, to rub, to anoint) or מָשַׁח (mashakh, to anoint). Unlike the verb χρίω (chriô), which emphasizes solemn or sacred anointing (notably of kings or priests), ἀλείφω focuses on the practical and daily act of applying a substance to the skin or body.
G0218.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament. Matthew, Mark, and Luke mention it to describe care for the body: the disciples heal the sick by anointing them (Mark 6:13), a sinful woman anoints Jesus' feet (Luke 7:38, 46), and the women prepare spices to anoint Jesus' body after his crucifixion (Mark 16:1). John refers twice to the anointing of Jesus by Mary at Jesus' feet (John 11:2; 12:3). James 5:14 uses it to prescribe the anointing of the sick in the context of prayer. The contexts vary: an offended gesture of hospitality, medical care, honor given to the dead, a mark of love and devotion.
G0218.portee: This verb invites the reader to see in anointing a body language that expresses honor, care, and love. The Gospels show how women and disciples express their attachment to Jesus through this concrete gesture. For James, the anointing of the sick is not magic, but a visible accompaniment of prayer, reminding us that faith is also lived through the body and actions. It is a word that brings salvation from the abstract realm to the sensitive and tangible realm.

sens: the crow of the rooster at dawn
the division of the night corresponding to this moment (third watch)
G0219.detail:
1. The cock's crow is the characteristic cry that the rooster makes at dawn. It is a natural sound, well known in Israel as in any agricultural country, marking the transition from night to day. In Mark 13:35, Jesus lists it as one of the possible moments when the master may return.
2. In the system of dividing the night hours in effect at the time of Jesus, the cock's crow designates the third watch of the night, the one that precedes dawn and sunrise. It is a concrete and recognizable time marker for all, especially for those who keep watch.
G0219.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "alektôr" (the rooster) and "phônê" (the voice or cry). It is a rare and very specific word, formed to precisely describe this moment of the night characterized by the crow of the rooster. It appears only once in the New Testament.
G0219.emploi: The word appears only once in the Gospels, in Mark 13:35. Jesus speaks to the disciples about his coming and the moments when it might occur: in the evening, at midnight, at the cock's crow, or in the morning. This enumeration reflects the four Roman watches of the night, and the cock's crow is the signal of the third watch. It is a natural and observable time marker, making the passage of time clear for all who lived in the countryside or tended flocks.
G0219.portee: The use of the cock's crow reminds us that Jesus speaks to his disciples in images they know well and that are part of their daily lives. This shows that he calls us to be watchful and ready, without knowing the day or the hour: we must remain attentive, like one who listens even in the darkness.

sens: Domestic bird known for its characteristic crow
Signal of dawn marked by its cry
Testimony of betrayal and denial
G0220.detail:
1. The rooster is a domestic bird known for its distinctive crow at dawn (Matthew 26:34: "before the rooster crows"). It is a common farm animal, familiar to Jesus' listeners.
2. In biblical culture, the crow of the rooster precisely marks dawn, the moment of transition from night to day (Mark 14:72). It thus becomes a natural signal of the coming of light.
3. For Peter and for the reader of the Gospels, the rooster symbolizes the moment of denial and shame: Jesus predicts that Peter will deny him before the rooster crows, and it is precisely the crow of the rooster that brings Peter back to his sin (Luke 22:60-61). The animal becomes the silent but unavoidable witness of Peter's failure.
G0220.origine: The Greek word ἀλέκτωρ is a poetic form of the word ἀλεκτρυών. It simply designates the domestic rooster. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) also uses it to refer to domestic animals. The word refers to the real animal, without mysterious etymology: it is the name given to the rooster in the spoken and written Greek of Jesus' time.
G0220.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the four Gospels, exclusively in the account of Peter's denial. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John all report Jesus' prophecy: before the rooster crows, Peter will deny him three times (Matthew 26:34, Mark 14:30, Luke 22:34, John 13:38). The fulfillment of this word is recounted by all four Evangelists: the rooster indeed crows (Matthew 26:74, Mark 14:68 and 14:72, Luke 22:60). In Mark, the rooster crows twice, corresponding to Jesus' version in Mark 14:30 ("before the rooster crows twice"). The rooster serves as a concrete and inevitable time marker of the moment when Jesus' word is fulfilled, awakening Peter's guilty conscience.
G0220.portee: The rooster teaches us that even our worst falls—denial—occur within the normal order of history, visible and a witness to God's plan. For Peter, this crow was a call to repentance: the innocent bird reminds us that it is never too late to acknowledge our fault and return to Jesus. The passage invites the reader to pray not to succumb, as Jesus asked Peter himself.

sens: a person native to or a resident of Alexandria
G0221.detail: 1. An Alexandrian is someone who comes from Alexandria, the great city of Egypt founded by Alexander the Great. In Acts 6:9, we encounter a synagogue of Alexandrians in Jerusalem: Jews from Alexandria who had settled in Israel and maintained their identity by grouping together by region of origin. In Acts 18:24, Apollos is described as "from Alexandria," a learned and eloquent Jew, highlighting the cultural and intellectual significance of this city in ancient Judaism.
G0221.origine: The word comes directly from the name Alexandria (Ἀλεξάνδρια in Greek), the capital of Hellenistic Egypt founded by the conqueror Alexander the Great around 330 BC. The Greek suffix -εύς denotes an inhabitant or native of a place, like an Athenian (-εύς) for someone from Athens. Alexandria was then one of the largest cities in the Mediterranean world, a major center of diaspora Judaism.
G0221.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of Luke. In one of the occurrences, it refers to members of a Jewish community organized by synagogue in Jerusalem (Acts 6:9): these Alexandrians opposed Stephen and brought him to trial. In the other, it describes Apollos (Acts 18:24), a particularly educated Jew well-versed in Scripture. These two usages show that Alexandria was an important source of educated Jews passionate about the Torah in the ancient world.
G0221.portee: The mention of the Alexandrians reminds us that the early Church was composed of Jews from all over the Mediterranean and diverse cultures. It also emphasizes the importance of Alexandria as a center of biblical learning: Apollos, although initially only familiar with the baptism of John, was already knowledgeable in the Scriptures, attesting to the tradition of rigorous biblical study that existed there. It is an invitation to recognize the richness of biblical thought in Hellenistic Judaism.

sens: Major port city in Egypt, capital of the Hellenistic kingdom of the Ptolemies
G0222.detail: Alexandria is the principal city of Egypt, founded by Alexander the Great on the Mediterranean coast. It is a major center of maritime trade and also an important cultural and religious hub where many Greek Jews live. In Acts, it appears as a port from which merchant ships sail across the Mediterranean: Paul boards a ship from Alexandria heading to Italy (Acts 27:6).
G0222.origine: The name comes from Alexander the Great (in Greek Ἀλέξανδρος), the founder of the city in the 4th century BC. The Greek adjective Ἀλεξανδρῖνος literally means "of Alexandria" or "Alexandrian"; it applies to anything that comes from or relates to this city. The corresponding Hebrew word from the Greek Old Testament does not exist, as Alexandria is a later Greek foundation.
G0222.emploi: Alexandria appears twice in Acts, in chapters 27 and 28, in the account of Paul's journey to Rome after his arrest. Acts 27:6 mentions a ship from Alexandria carrying wheat and passengers to Italy: it is on this ship that Paul is transferred with other prisoners. Acts 28:11 again cites a ship from Alexandria that wintered in Malta. These mentions reflect the importance of Alexandria as a trading port and crossroads of Mediterranean commerce in the first century.
G0222.portee: Alexandria symbolizes for the reader the extent of the Christian presence and the connection between the Jewish world and the Greco-Roman world. The city was also known for its schools of biblical exegesis and its dynamic Jewish community. This geographical detail from Luke reminds us that the Gospel spreads in the major urban and commercial centers of the time, and that divine providence uses the routes of this vast interconnected world.

sens: Son of Simon of Cyrene
G0223G.detail: 1. Alexander is the son of Simon of Cyrene, the man whom the soldiers forced to carry the cross of Jesus on the way to Golgotha (Mark 15:21). The fact that the Gospel names him, along with his brother Rufus, suggests that he was known to the early Christian communities, perhaps as a disciple or respected figure in the early Church.
G0223G.origine: The name "Alexander" comes from the Greek *Alexandros*, composed of *alexo* (to repel, defend) and *andros* (man): literally "one who repels men" or "defender." It is a common Greek name in antiquity, notably borne by Alexander the Great. In the New Testament, several characters bear this name.
G0223G.emploi: Alexander appears only once in the Segond 1910, in Mark 15:21. He is presented as the son of Simon of Cyrene, the Cyrenian whom Matthew, Mark, and Luke all mention as having carried the cross of Jesus. Only Mark names his two sons, Alexander and Rufus, indicating that these names were significant to the readers of his Gospel — likely because they had converted and were known to the Church.

sens: Relative of the high priest in Jerusalem
Influential member of the Jewish priestly family
G0223H.detail:
1. Alexander is a Greek name, that of a man from the family of the high priest, mentioned when Peter and John are questioned in Jerusalem (Acts 4:6). He sits among the Jewish religious leaders who interrogate the apostles after the healing of the lame man at the temple gate.
2. His status as a relative of the high priest indicates that he is part of the Jewish priestly aristocracy, a powerful group that controls the functioning of the temple and opposes the message of the disciples.
G0223H.origine: Alexander comes from ancient Greek meaning "one who repels enemies" (from alexein, to repel, and andros, man). This name was extremely popular in the Greco-Roman world, notably borne by Alexander the Great. In the biblical context, it is a Greek name borne by a high-ranking Jew, reflecting Greek influence in the Jewish priestly families of the first century.
G0223H.emploi: The entry documents only one use of the name Alexander in the Segond: Acts 4:6, where he is cited alongside Annas, Caiaphas, and John, all major figures of the Sanhedrin (the council of elders). He is expressly identified as a relative of the high priest. Other passages mention different Alexanders (the son of Simon the Cyrenian, a silversmith, a Jew in Ephesus), but this usage isolates the member of the priestly family here.
G0223H.portee: This mention reveals that the opposition to the apostolic message came from the highest echelons of Jewish religious authority, from those whom God had once chosen to lead His people. It reminds the reader that the rejection of the Gospel, even by religious authorities, cannot stand against the power of the resurrection of Jesus.

sens: Jew who intervened during the riot against Paul in Ephesus
G0223I.detail: 1. A Jewish man who, during the riot against the apostle Paul in Ephesus, was pushed forward by the crowd of Jews to speak and calm the spirits. He raised his hand to be heard but did not get the chance to express himself in front of the hostile crowd (Acts 19:33).
G0223I.origine: Alexander is a very common Greek name in antiquity, composed of elements meaning "to defend" and "man" or "people." It literally designates one who "defends men." This name has been borne by several important figures in the New Testament and in Jewish and Christian circles of the time.
G0223I.emploi: The name Alexander appears only once in the provided passage from Acts 19:33, where it identifies a Jew from the community of Ephesus. His role in this account remains limited: he was well-known or recognized among the Jews to be designated to the crowd to defend his fellow Jews during the great riot sparked by Paul's preaching. The mention of his attempt to speak ("making a sign with his hand") suggests some authority or status among the Jews of Ephesus, although the context indicates that he did not succeed in gaining a hearing from the unruly crowd.

sens: metal worker who works with copper
opponent of the apostle Paul
G0223J.detail:
1. Alexander is a skilled worker in copper — an important trade in ancient cities for making everyday objects, tools, coins, and religious utensils. In 2 Timothy 4:14, Paul refers to him as "Alexander the coppersmith."
2. This man opposed the apostle Paul and his message with hostility. Paul mentions him among those who persecuted him, and he even "delivered him to Satan" as a serious disciplinary measure, hoping to bring him to his senses (1 Timothy 1:20). He is an example of the rejection and hostility that Christian preachers have faced.
G0223J.origine: The Greek name Alexandros literally means "one who repels men" or "protector of men" (from the Greek alexein = to repel, and aner = man). It is a classical Greek name, notably famous due to Alexander the Great. In the Bible, this name refers to an ordinary man whose opposition to the Christian message is all that is remembered.
G0223J.emploi: Alexander the coppersmith appears twice in Paul's letters to Timothy, written toward the end of the apostle's life. In 1 Timothy 1:20, Paul lists him among the heretics who "have made shipwreck" of their faith — alongside Hymenaeus — and he had to exclude them from the church's fellowship to bring them to order. In 2 Timothy 4:14, Paul revisits him a few years later, describing him as a malicious opponent who has severely harmed him. Both passages show a man who has abandoned the faith and actively opposed Paul.
G0223J.portee: Alexander reminds us that the Christian faith encounters hostility, even from those who initially confessed it. His example warns believers of the possibility of making "shipwreck" of their faith (1 Timothy 1:19) — turning away from Christ and becoming opponents. This calls for vigilance and prayer to remain steadfast in the Gospel.

sens: Fine powder obtained by grinding grains, particularly wheat
Basic ingredient for making bread or other foods
Biblical image of what is mixed and transformed by an invisible force
G0224.detail:
1. Flour is the fine powder obtained by grinding wheat or other grains. It is a very concrete raw material, commonplace in the biblical Middle East. It is a key ingredient in bread, the fundamental food.

2. In the parable of the leaven (Matthew 13:33; Luke 13:21), Jesus speaks of a woman who mixes leaven into three measures of flour. The leaven — a fermenting substance — spreads invisibly throughout the flour until the dough rises completely. Here, flour symbolizes the material upon which a hidden and powerful force acts, transforming it from within.
G0224.origine: The Greek word ἄλευρον comes from the verb ἀλεύω (aleuô), which means "to grind." Thus, etymologically, it refers to what is ground. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it is rendered by קֶמַח (qemaḥ), which also refers to wheat flour. The word describes the concrete product of mill work, used since ancient times to prepare bread.
G0224.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in the same parable reported by Matthew and Luke. Jesus uses it to teach how the kingdom of heaven operates: discreetly yet irresistibly, transforming from within. It is a very simple word, designating a material reality that every listener was well acquainted with. The parable is not technical; it speaks the language of everyday cooking to reveal a spiritual truth.
G0224.portee: This image of flour and leaven shows that the kingdom of God does not advance by force or external splendor, but through a hidden and progressive action that transforms everything it touches. Like leaven in flour, the Gospel works silently and changes reality from within. It is an encouraging promise for disciples: God's work is accomplished even when it is not visible.

sens: What is real, what truly exists, as opposed to what is false or apparent
The entirety of Christian doctrine, the teaching of Christ and the Gospel
Authenticity, sincerity, integrity of heart and character
The conformity between what is said and reality, honesty in speech
G0225.detail:
1. Truth is primarily the reality that lies behind appearances — what is truly real. When Jesus says, "I am the truth" (John 14:6), he asserts that in him manifests the ultimate reality, the true essence of God. God's judgment is exercised "according to the truth" (Romans 2:2): he judges according to the reality of things, without illusion or appearance.
2. Truth also refers to the entirety of Christian doctrine, what God has revealed and what the Gospel teaches. "Obeying the truth" (Galatians 5:7) means following the teaching of Christ and the Gospel. Those who stray from the path of faith "prevent themselves from obeying the truth."
3. Truth is also a moral quality: it is sincerity, integrity of heart, uprightness. Speaking the truth is not just avoiding lies in words; it is having an honest, authentic heart, without duplicity. The devil "is a liar and the father of lies" (John 8:44): there is no truth in him, either externally or internally.
4. Finally, truth in speech is the concordance between what is said and reality: to speak with truth is to say what is, frankly and without evasion. Paul claims to speak "the truth" when he candidly discusses the persecutions he has endured (2 Corinthians 12:6).
G0225.origine: The Greek word alètheia comes from the verb meaning "not to forget, to remember": truth is what is remembered, what remains stable and enduring, as opposed to forgetfulness and illusion. Jesus asserts: "You will know the truth" (John 8:32) — it is about a true and lasting knowledge. In the Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew "emet," which evokes solidity, faithfulness, certainty: truth is what one can rely on, what does not deceive.
G0225.emploi: The word alètheia appears 109 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels of John and in Paul's epistles. In John, truth is almost always linked to the person of Jesus and the knowledge of God: it is not merely an abstract doctrine, but a living reality in Jesus Christ. In Paul, truth often refers to the Gospel, the Christian doctrine that must be defended against false teachings (see Galatians 2:5). In the synoptic Gospels, Christ's adversaries acknowledge that he "teaches according to the truth" (Matthew 22:16), even though they refuse to follow him. The word is also used to describe the sincerity and integrity required in Christian life: "Put on truth" (Ephesians 6:14), meaning live in authenticity and honesty.
G0225.portee: Understanding biblical truth means recognizing that what truly matters is not appearance or opinion, but reality as God sees it. For the Christian, this means two things: first, to embrace Jesus as the incarnate truth, the complete revelation of God; secondly, to cultivate sincerity and integrity in one's own life, rejecting lies and hypocrisy, and seeking to live in accordance with the reality of the Gospel. It is a call to transparency of heart and to conformity between what one claims to believe and how one lives.

sens: express what is true
speak with sincerity and loyalty
oppose someone out of love by telling them what is right
G0226.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to express what is true, to speak the truth (Galatians 4:16: "Have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?"). It is the opposite of lying or concealing.
2. It also carries the idea of speaking with sincerity and loyalty, without evasion or calculation. One who speaks the truth exposes their heart without artifice.
3. In Ephesians 4:15, "speaking the truth in love," the word takes on a broader tone: it is not only about speaking well, but about living and acting in the truth, manifesting what is right and faithful in all of life.
G0226.origine: The verb comes from the adjective "true" (ἀληθής), which is itself formed from a root meaning "not to hide, not to forget." The truth is what is not veiled, what does not evade. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, this verb translates Hebrew words related to righteousness ("just judgment"), peace ("to fulfill"), and integrity.
G0226.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul's epistles. In Galatians 4:16, Paul defends his right to speak the truth even if it hurts: being a friend to God's people does not prevent one from rebuking them frankly. In Ephesians 4:15, he encourages Christians to "speak the truth in love" — in other words, to grow spiritually through honest speech tempered with love. Both passages show that speaking the truth is not brutality, but an act of courage and faithfulness toward others.
G0226.portee: This verb places the demand for sincerity at the heart of Christian life. For Paul, speaking the truth is an act of courage: it can make you an enemy in the eyes of those who do not want to hear it. But it is also an act of love, provided it is motivated by charity. It invites the Christian to reject lying and flattery, and to seek a just word that builds up.

sens: Conforming to reality, to what has really happened or exists
Trustworthy, telling the truth
Authentic, sincere, without deception
G0227.detail:
1. That which conforms to the reality of facts. When John bears witness to Jesus, this testimony "is true" (John 5:31) — it accurately reports what happened, not an invention. Similarly, the proverb about the dog returning to its vomit is "true" (2 Peter 2:22): it is a real observation of nature. The bread that Jesus gives is "true food" (John 6:55) — not just an image, but something real that truly nourishes.
2. A "true" person is trustworthy because they tell the truth. The disciples come to tell Jesus: "you are true," meaning that he teaches without lying, without contradicting the truth (Matthew 22:16). A "true" teaching or testimony is not deceitful; it corresponds to what is.
3. That which is authentic and sincere, without pretense. One who "bears witness" to what they have seen with their own eyes gives a true testimony (John 19:35) — they do not fabricate a story; they report what they have observed themselves.
G0227.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "not to hide, to make manifest." A "true" word is a word that makes reality visible: it does not conceal it; it shows it. The Bible uses it to translate the Hebrew word meaning "faithfulness, solidity, certainty" — that which can be known and counted on. It is a word related to trust: what is true can be believed.
G0227.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the New Testament, mostly in John, who uses it to speak of the word of Jesus and his testimony. It designates what conforms to reality: a fact reported accurately (John 10:41), a proverb that corresponds to observation (2 Peter 2:22), a food that truly nourishes (John 6:55). It also applies to people: someone is "true" if they are truthful, if they teach without lies or evasion (Matthew 22:16, Mark 12:14). John 3:33 says that "believing the testimony of Jesus" means recognizing that "God is true" — which means that God is entirely trustworthy. It is the word of established facts and reliable words.
G0227.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the testimony given about Jesus in the Gospel is not a pious legend: it is a faithful account of what really happened. Trusting the Gospel means believing that the one who testifies reports the truth, without embellishment or invention. It also invites the disciple to seek the truth in their own life — not to settle for appearances, but to align their life with what is real and true.

sens: that which truly exists, as opposed to what is false, counterfeit, or illusory
that which is authentic, trustworthy, without deception
that which is in accordance with its true nature or ideal essence
that which is true in a spiritual or eternal sense, beyond earthly appearances
G0228.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what is real, true, opposed to lies or imitation. John 19:35 affirms that the disciple's testimony is "true" — it is an honest account of the facts.
2. It qualifies what is authentic and reliable: Revelation 16:7 speaks of God's judgments as "true and just," meaning just in reality, trustworthy.
3. It especially designates what is true in its deep nature, its essence. Hebrews 9:24 contrasts the "genuine" sanctuary (heaven itself, real and eternal) with the earthly sanctuary (a mere imitation). John 6:32 calls the bread from heaven "true" in contrast to earthly bread — the true bread is that which truly nourishes, spiritually.
4. Finally, it expresses the ultimate spiritual truth: John 17:3 names God as "the only true God," emphasizing his unique and definitive character, beyond anything that claims divinity.
G0228.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἀληθ- (aleth-), which literally means "that which does not remain hidden" or "that which appears." It is formed as an adjective "ideal" (comparable to how we say "the genuine king" for the authentic king as opposed to an impostor). In biblical Hebrew, it generally corresponds to the word אֱמֶת (emet), which means "truth" and "faithfulness" — that which holds, that which can be trusted.
G0228.emploi: This word appears 26 times in the New Testament, mostly in John (8 times) and in Revelation (11 times), as well as in Hebrews. John uses it to distinguish spiritual reality from earthly appearance or copy: the true bread (6:32), the true vine (15:1), the true God (17:3). In Hebrews, it contrasts the true sanctuary (heaven, 9:24) with earthly figures. Revelation applies it to God and Christ (Revelation 3:7, 19:11) to affirm that they are truly what they are, without flaw or imitation. The meaning does not vary much: it always concerns the authentic, the real, the definitive, as opposed to the provisional or counterfeit.
G0228.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to distinguish what truly lasts from what is temporary or deceptive. Understanding that God is "the only true God" (John 17:3) and that Christ is the "true vine" (John 15:1) roots faith in eternal reality, beyond the appearances of the world. It is a call to seek what is authentic in the relationship with God, rather than being satisfied with earthly imitations.

sens: to grind grain between two millstones to make flour
to work at the mill
to be engaged in a daily task
G0229.detail:
1. The word refers to the action of grinding grain between two millstones to obtain flour. It is a manual and physical labor, typical of ancient daily life (Matthew 24:41, Luke 17:35).
2. To grind also evokes the activity itself, the work at the mill, often done by two women together: it is a common and regular task, symbolizing the ordinary occupation of life (Luke 17:35).
3. By extension, the word represents any form of routine and daily work, which absorbs attention and effort — making its use in Jesus' words about the end times particularly striking: two women are engaged in their ordinary labor when judgment occurs.
G0229.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning to grind or reduce to powder. The basic image is that of the millstone, an essential tool in ancient societies. In Hebrew, the verb טָחַן (taḥan) carries the same meaning and also appears in biblical texts to refer to this work. The form used here is that of the common dialect (κοινή) of the New Testament period.
G0229.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in two parallel sayings of Jesus announcing his return. In Matthew 24:41 and Luke 17:35, two women will be grinding together at the mill: one will be taken and the other left. These two occurrences use exactly the same context — a scene of ordinary life that will suddenly shift during the final judgment. The choice of this verb is not trivial: it paints human life in its banal routine, forgetful of eternity.
G0229.portee: This word reminds us that the return of Christ can occur during the most ordinary and consuming occupations of daily life. It invites everyone to remain vigilant, not by being inactive, but by keeping the mind attentive to God's will even in the midst of responsibilities. It is a call to live with sobriety and expectation, without allowing earthly tasks to obscure spiritual reality.

sens: with truth, without lie
in a certain and sure manner
in a way that deserves trust and assent
G0230.detail:
1. This adverb asserts that what is said corresponds to reality: there is no deception or illusion. When the centurion says, "Truly, this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39), he acknowledges as true and real what he has just testified to by witnessing how Jesus died.
2. The word expresses a certainty that imposes itself on the speaker: there is no possible doubt. To Nicodemus, Jesus declares, "I tell you the truth, unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3) — it is a word on which one can rely for absolute truth.
3. To say something "truly" also asks to be believed, because what is affirmed deserves credence. John 4:42 shows this nuance: the Samaritans say, "We know that he is truly the Savior of the world" — their faith rests on what they have personally verified.
G0230.origine: The word comes from the adjective "true" (ἀληθής). In biblical Hebrew, it often corresponds to "amen," the word of confirmation and commitment to the truth (see Jeremiah 28:6). It is the same word that Christians pronounce when they say "Amen" at the end of a prayer: they confirm that it is true and that they adhere to it.
G0230.emploi: Jesus uses this adverb 13 times in the four Gospels to introduce his most important words: his teachings on the Kingdom, on eternal life, on his identity. It is his way of signaling, "Listen carefully, what I say is absolutely true." Other characters in the biblical narrative use it to publicly acknowledge a reality that imposes itself on them: the centurion affirming that Jesus is the Son of God (Mark 15:39), the disciples confessing their faith (Matthew 14:33), the Samaritans testifying to Jesus' identity (John 4:42). It is a word that appears especially in decisive moments when the truth is revealed.
G0230.portee: For the Christian reader, this adverb is an invitation to give assent. Every time Jesus says, "I tell you the truth," he calls for faith: what he affirms is absolutely trustworthy. It is also a model for our own speech: to speak "truly" is to renounce deception and commit to the truth.

sens: one who fishes, who catches fish
one who captures men for God (figurative sense)
G0231.detail:
1. A fisherman is a man whose profession is to fish, that is, to catch fish in the water. Simon Peter and Andrew, whom Jesus calls by the Sea of Galilee, are professional fishermen: they cast nets into the sea and formed a team of fishing workers (Matthew 4:18; Luke 5:2 even shows the fishermen washing their nets after work).
2. Jesus uses the word in a figurative sense: "I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:19; Mark 1:17). He takes the image of the net and capture to say that his disciples will have the mission of bringing men to faith, just as one attracts fish. It is a call to transform their skills into spiritual work.
G0231.origine: The Greek word comes from the root that designates the sea (ἅλς). A fisherman is literally one who works at the sea. In Hebrew, the Bible uses the words דָּג (fish) and דַּוָּג (fisher) for the same reality. The Greek word has thus retained the image of the close link between the sea and the one who draws his food and income from it.
G0231.emploi: The word appears only five times in the New Testament, always to refer to the first disciples: Peter, Andrew, and their associates who fished on the Sea of Galilee. The first three Gospels all recount this calling by the sea. Jesus meets these fishermen in the exercise of their profession, at the moment they are working (Matthew 4:18; Mark 1:16; Luke 5:2). When Jesus says, "I will make you fishers of men," he plays on this word: he keeps the profession (fisherman) but transfers the target (from fish to men). This wordplay was meaningful for the men Jesus was drawing to himself by calling them to a new service.
G0231.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God calls people in their reality and profession, not by extracting them from the world but by transforming the meaning of their work. Peter and Andrew did not cease to be fishermen: Jesus gave their skill and dedication a new spiritual significance. This also speaks to the Christian disciple: our task is to "fish" for men to faith, that is, to attract them with patience and wisdom towards Jesus.

sens: To catch fish from the water with a net or a line
To engage in the profession of fisherman
To engage in an activity without immediate success
G0232.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very concrete: to cast a net into the water or use a line to catch fish. This is the work of professional fishermen, like Simon Peter and his companions who practiced this trade before following Jesus (John 21:3).

2. The verb refers to the activity itself, the profession of fisherman practiced regularly. Peter and John return to their nets at night, which was the usual practice on the Sea of Tiberias at that time.

3. By extension, the word can evoke any action that consists of searching for something in uncertainty, without guarantee of result — like that night when the disciples worked hard but caught nothing (John 21:3).
G0232.origine: The Greek word ἁλιεύω comes from ἁλιεύς ("fisherman") and ἅλς ("salt, sea"). The root refers to the sea and work in a marine environment. In Hebrew, the verb דָּיַג (dag, "to fish") belongs to the same semantic family, hence the translation in the Septuagint. It is a concrete word related to the daily life of coastal peoples.
G0232.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in John 21:3, during the appearance of the Resurrected One to the disciples by the lake. Peter announces his intention to return to his former profession: "I am going fishing." This unique usage is significant because it marks the return of the disciples to their former life, before the Resurrected One calls them to their new vocation. It is a moment of transition where the apostles are still hesitant about their future direction. The context emphasizes the failure of the night — they catch nothing — which prepares for the miracle of the miraculous catch that Jesus will perform in the morning.
G0232.portee: This word reminds us that the first disciples had an ordinary life, a manual profession, before Jesus called them. It also speaks to the doubt and hesitation that can arise after a crisis of faith: Peter returns to what he knows. Finally, the contrast between the failure of human fishing and the miracle that Jesus performs afterward teaches us that without Christ, our efforts remain barren, but with Him, abundance becomes possible.

sens: To add salt to something to season or preserve it
In a figurative sense, to purify or refine through suffering and trial
To make flavorful or invigorating in one's Christian testimony
G0233.detail:
